selection.reason: Impact scored and summarised by Gemini. (rated before the current eligibility rules; kept)

summary: The Pell Grant Preservation and Expansion Act of 2026 makes changes to the Federal Pell Grant program and other student financial assistance rules under the Higher Education Act of 1965. The bill increases maximum Pell Grant award amounts over several years, transitions funding to mandatory appropriations, expands eligibility to certain non-citizen students and students receiving means-tested benefits, restores eligibility for students with outside scholarships, extends the maximum semesters of eligibility, and updates rules regarding satisfactory academic progress.

affected_groups.effect: Eligible for higher maximum Pell Grant award amounts, increased total semesters of eligibility (up to 18 semesters), and restored eligibility if they receive outside scholarships.

Assigned a student aid index of -$1,500 if they or their parents/spouse received benefits under a means-tested federal benefit program during the previous two-year period, qualifying them for increased Pell Grant aid.
Made explicitly eligible for federal student aid if they meet defined educational, military service, or deferred action criteria.
Subject to updated institutional warning and probation standards, with opportunities to regain eligibility or reset eligibility after leaving school for two years.
affected_groups.group: Students failing to maintain satisfactory academic progress

affected_groups.effect: Required to update and maintain specific satisfactory academic progress policies, evaluation periods, student communications, and consumer testing compliance.

key_provisions: Sets the total maximum Federal Pell Grant award at $10,000 for the 2026-2027 award year, scaling up annually to $15,000 for the 2031-2032 award year with subsequent adjustments based on the Consumer Price Index.
Appropriates mandatory funds out of the Treasury as necessary for fiscal year 2026 and subsequent years to provide Pell Grants.

Provides an increased Federal Pell Grant award for students with a student aid index of less than zero, and sets the student aid index to -$1,500 for applicants who received benefits under a means-tested federal benefit program within the previous two years.
Expands federal student aid eligibility to include Dreamer students meeting specific criteria or hardship exceptions.
Increases the total semesters of Federal Pell Grant eligibility from 12 semesters to 18 semesters.

Revises satisfactory academic progress policies, establishes rules for financial aid warnings and probation, and allows certain students who leave school for two years to reset their financial aid eligibility up to two times.
Removes provisions that made students whose total non-federal grants and scholarships equaled or exceeded their cost of attendance ineligible for the Federal Pell Grant.
missing_information: Exact total federal budget costs and long-term fiscal impact projections.
Specific administrative guidelines for implementing the Dreamer student hardship exceptions.
Detailed definitions of all means-tested federal benefit programs referenced via external statutes.
summary_detail.plain_summary: The Pell Grant Preservation and Expansion Act of 2026 makes changes to the Federal Pell Grant program and other student financial assistance rules under the Higher Education Act of 1965. The bill increases maximum Pell Grant award amounts over several years, transitions funding to mandatory appropriations, expands eligibility to certain non-citizen students and students receiving means-tested benefits, restores eligibility for students with outside scholarships, extends the maximum semesters of eligibility, and updates rules regarding satisfactory academic progress.
summary_detail.significance: The legislation alters federal student financial aid by changing the funding structure of the Pell Grant program from discretionary/partial to mandatory appropriations that grow with inflation, while increasing maximum award levels and expanding eligibility rules to cover new groups of students and longer periods of study. The score for significance is 85 due to the nationwide scope affecting millions of federal student aid recipients and institutions of higher education.
